questions.q: What is the central metaphor in Nagarjun's poem "लकड़ियों में आग" and what two entities does it connect?
questions.a: The central metaphor is "fire hidden in wood" (लकड़ियों में आग), connecting the latent revolutionary consciousness in the oppressed masses (wood) to the inevitable uprising (fire) that will consume the exploitative system. A wrong answer that identifies only "fire" or "wood" separately, or connects fire to "nature" instead of "social revolution," reveals the student has not grasped the metaphor's socio-political function and is reading literally rather than allegorically.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet says "एल्लज निजर" (foolish, broken) in the first stanza and how this description sets up the poem's central argument.
questions.a: The phrase describes the wood as seemingly useless and discarded, mirroring how the ruling class views the poor as worthless and powerless; this sets up the poem's argument by establishing the deceptive appearance that the exploiters believe, which the poet will overturn by revealing the hidden fire. A wrong answer that treats "एल्लज निजर" as mere physical description of dry wood misses the irony: the poet adopts the oppressor's vocabulary only to subvert it, showing the student has not understood the poem's rhetorical strategy of ironic reversal.

questions.q: Apply the fire-in-wood metaphor to a contemporary Indian context: identify a specific marginalized community and describe what the "wood," "fire," and "spark" would represent in their struggle, using the poem's logic.
questions.a: For landless agricultural laborers in Bihar: the "wood" is their suppressed labor and dignity, the "fire" is their collective consciousness of rights (e.g., minimum wage awareness), and the "spark" is a triggering event like a landlord's atrocity or a union organizer's speech. Steps: (1) Identify the dormant group (wood), (2) Identify the latent energy (fire), (3) Identify the catalyst (spark), (4) Map each to the poem's three-stanza progression. A wrong answer that chooses a middle-class protest or separates the spark from the community's own agency reveals the student cannot transfer the metaphor's structural logic — specifically that the fire arises from within the wood, not from outside.

questions.q: Analyze how the shift from third-person observation in stanza 1 ("लकड़ियों में आग") to first-person declaration in stanza 2 ("मैं चसदज ग्वाँ...") to prophetic future tense in stanza 3 ("रहजक फौजक...") structures the poem's thematic argument.
questions.a: The progression enacts the theme: stanza 1 presents the objective reality (fire exists in wood regardless of perception), stanza 2 inserts the poet as witness-participant aligning with the oppressed ("I am with the insignificant"), and stanza 3 projects the inevitable historical outcome (the "careless world" will be consumed). This three-stage structure — diagnosis, solidarity, prophecy — mirrors the revolutionary process itself. A wrong answer that treats the stanzas as merely descriptive, or misses the shift from "is" to "will be," reveals the student cannot analyze how poetic structure encodes thematic argument.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Nagarjun's poem is pessimistic because it predicts destruction." Defend your judgment using specific lines and the distinction between destruction of the oppressive order versus destruction of the oppressed.
questions.a: The claim is false; the poem is revolutionary-optimistic. The "destruction" targets the "ग़फ़लत" (complacent world) of the exploiters ("रहजक फौजक" — the careless army/rulers), while the "चसदज" (insignificant ones) are the agents of renewal. The fire purifies; it does not annihilate the wood but releases its energy. A wrong answer that agrees with the claim reveals the student conflates revolutionary violence with nihilism and cannot distinguish between the poem's targets (the oppressive structure) and its heroes (the oppressed), missing the poem's clear moral framework.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in Hindi that extends the poem's metaphor to a modern context (e.g., digital activism, climate justice, student movements), maintaining the original's rhythm and the fire-in-wood logic.
questions.a: Example: "स्मार्टफोन की ठूँठ में धधकता सवाल / उँगलियों की चिंगारी से जलेगा जाल / ग़फ़लत की दीवारें ढहेंगी आज / युवा लकड़ियों की आग बनेगी काज।" A good answer maps wood→suppressed questions, spark→digital action, fire→collective uprising, and targets the complacent system. A poor answer that writes a generic motivational verse without the metaphor's causal logic (spark-from-within, inevitable consumption of the old order) reveals the student has not internalized the poem's structural metaphor as a generative template.
